Read IN FULL: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-marcel-a-n-navarro-Dev/646bc8ac-afb6-41b4-8d24-dcbaf28144cd/scratchpad/agents_closedloop.txt

This is the complete agent-transcript record of ONE Claude Code session in which Marcel Navarro (FED Lead on the Zimmermann PWA Kit) ran a closed-loop multi-agent workflow to build the "PDP Static Product Info" user story (SFCC-89). It spawned **97 subagents**. Marcel considers this his biggest success and wants the workflow it used encoded into a reusable skill.

Each agent appears as: a header with `type=` and `task:` (its description), then `>>> PROMPT GIVEN` and `>>> FINAL REPORT`.

READ THE WHOLE FILE (~275,000 tokens) in sequential slices with Read offset/limit. Keep a running reconstruction; discard raw text as you go.

The loop Marcel described running is: an **orchestrator** (also scope-checking to spec, neither under nor over) → **builder/implementer** → **tester** (deploying subagents across different aspects) → **scorer** (marks complete OR returns to implementer, looping until passed) → plus a **tracker** that watches the whole flow and feeds improvements back into the other four while the loop still runs.

Reconstruct what ACTUALLY happened, not what was intended. Report:

**1. THE ACTUAL TOPOLOGY.** What roles really existed, in what order, who handed off to whom. Did the five roles appear as described, or did it work differently? Map it. Note `spawnDepth` values — did agents spawn agents?

**2. THE ROLE PROMPTS.** For each distinct role, quote the actual prompt language Marcel (or the orchestrator) used to brief it. This is the single most valuable output — we want to reuse his real wording.

**3. THE LOOP DYNAMICS.** How many rounds? What did the scorer/verifier actually reject, and why? Quote specific rejections. Did anything loop more than twice? Did any loop fail to converge?

**4. WHAT THE TESTER CHECKED.** The concrete angles/aspects the testing agents were told to cover, and which ones actually caught real defects. Quote the defects found.

**5. WHERE IT BROKE DOWN.** Agents that returned useless, redundant, or wrong output. Duplicated work. Contradictions between agents. Anything Marcel had to intervene on manually.

**6. THE PASS CRITERIA.** How was "done" defined and judged? Quote the actual criteria used. Was it consistent across steps?

**7. WHAT TO REUSE VERBATIM.** Given all of the above, list the specific prompt fragments, role definitions, and check-lists that are worth lifting directly into a reusable skill — and separately, what should NOT be carried forward because it demonstrably didn't work.

OUTPUT: a structured report against those seven headings. Quote liberally — the actual prompt text is the deliverable. Be concrete about counts and rounds.

|---|---|

Atoms and molecules: **all built, all consumed by the footer.** Variants/states: **substantially complete, with three gaps** — `trailing` and `value`/`defaultValue` on `ZimmTextInput`, `disabled` on `ZimmInputAction`, `secondary × fullWidth` on `ZimmButton`. I've read all 11,194 lines. Here is the reconstruction.

---

# THE CLOSED-LOOP SESSION, RECONSTRUCTED

## 0. Two corrections to the brief, before anything else

**This session is not SFCC-89.** The file header reads `SESSION 652997c6-662c-4608-bb47-e37b77ba106b — ZIMM - PR #55 — 97 agents`. The work is **SFCC-55 "Global Footer UI"** (PR #55 closed, superseded by **PR #59**, merged 2026-08-24). `SFCC-55` appears 117 times; `SFCC-89` appears 15 times, always as *someone else's branch* being checked for atom reuse, or as the branch Marcel happened to be sitting on days later. If the skill is meant to encode "the SFCC-89 workflow," it is being built from the wrong session.

**The five roles as described do not exist in this transcript.** Every one of the 97 agents is `type=general-purpose` (89), `type=Explore` (6), or `type=fork` (2). There is **zero** use of `zm-orchestrator`, `zm-implementer`, `zm-tester`, `zm-scorer`, `zm-tracker`, or `zm-planner` — those agent definitions exist in the current environment but were written *after* this session, as a codification of it. What actually ran was a different, and in places better, shape.

**Timeline:** 08-21 (28 agents), 08-24 (48), 08-25 (20), 08-27 (1). Depths: 64 at depth 1, 31 at depth 2, 2 at depth 3.

---

# 1. THE ACTUAL TOPOLOGY

Agents did spawn agents — 33 of 97 ran at depth ≥2. But **subagent spawning was never part of the loop design**; it was ad-hoc delegation by depth-1 agents that hit something they couldn't settle. Marcel was the orchestrator throughout, by hand, from the top-level session.

The session is **seven distinct sequential structures**, not one loop.

### Phase A — Rule extraction, then a scope-partitioned audit fan-out (08-21, agents 2–6)

One agent extracts a checkable ruleset from two source docs. Then **four parallel auditors partitioned by concern, not by file**:

| Agent | Scope | Explicit exclusion |
|---|---|---|
| A | Naming & structure | "Do not audit imports, TypeScript typing, or test coverage — other agents own those." |
| B | Import analysis | "Do not audit naming, TypeScript typing, or test coverage." |
| C | TypeScript typing | "Do not audit naming, imports, or test coverage." |
| D | Test & story coverage | "Do not audit naming, imports, or TypeScript." |

### Phase B — A second, wider audit fan-out (agents 7–12)

Six agents, same partition-by-concern, plus two new axes the first pass lacked: **Jira AC conformance** and **FED playbook/manual conformance**. This is the closest thing in the session to Marcel's "orchestrator scope-checks to spec, neither under nor over."

### Phase C — THE 4-STAGE PIPELINE (agents 13–19) — the real closed loop

This is the part worth encoding. It is announced in every prompt as `"STAGE n of a 4-stage pipeline"`.

```
Phase B audits emit ~13 CLAIMS (M1, M2, S1–S11)
        ↓
STAGE 1  ×3 agents, partitioned by claim-cluster    (validate BY EXECUTION)
        ↓  only CONFIRMED claims pass through
STAGE 2  ×3 agents, partitioned by FILE OWNERSHIP    (implement + prove)
        ↓  all three finish → exclusive access
STAGE 3  ×1 agent, "you are the adversary"           (regression + interaction hunt)
        ↓
STAGE 4  commit-check — NAMED IN THE DESIGN, NEVER SPAWNED
```

Stage 4 exists only in the pipeline's own self-description (`"validate → implement → regress → commit-check"`). No agent ran it. Marcel did it himself.

**Stage 2's three agents were partitioned by file, with the partition stated in each prompt and enforced by the agents themselves** — every Stage 2 report ends with an annotated `git status --porcelain` marking each dirty file `← MINE` or `← sibling`.

### Phase D — Wave 1 / Wave 2 adversarial reconciliation (agents 21–28)

Four parallel Wave-1 agents on **deliberately opposed questions**: scope ledger (what did we build), cost of carry (what does the extra weight cost), opportunity cost (what's *missing*, explicitly framed as "the COUNTERWEIGHT"), and **audit the audit** (was this loop worth running). Then one Wave-2 agent whose entire job is to attack them.

### Phase E — Comprehension fan-out on a third party's commits (agents 29–36)

Six domain agents mapping what a colleague ("Tim Lavelle", 14 commits) changed. Prompts explicitly say `"GOAL IS COMPREHENSION, NOT AUDIT. Deliver an explanation... Not a findings list."`

### Phase F — The document loop (agents 37–45, 66, 95, 96)

`fork` writes a 750-line guide → **one pedagogy reviewer forbidden from opening the repo** → **six parallel depth-2 fact-checkers, one per document section** → one independent whole-doc fact-checker with no prior context → rewrite → re-fact-check → **content-loss audit against backups**.

### Phase G — The CodeRabbit V&V loop (agents 46–70) — the second real loop

```
14 CodeRabbit findings
   ↓  split 4 ways
V&V agents (verify each claim from scratch, verdict FIX/DECLINE/DEFER)
   ↓
"Audit the verdicts against Tim's precedent"  ×3 — a META-REVIEW of the reviewers
   ↓  2 of 8 declines OVERTURNED, 2 of 6 FIX verdicts OVERTURNED
implement
   ↓
"Independently verify / Adversarially verify" ×5, no prior context
```

**Where Marcel's five roles map, honestly:**

| Marcel's role | What actually existed |
|---|---|
| Orchestrator (scope-check to spec) | Marcel himself + Phase B's "Jira AC conformance" and "FED playbook conformance" agents + Wave-1's scope ledger |
| Builder / implementer | Stage 2 ×3, file-partitioned |
| Tester (multiple aspects) | Two things fused: the **audit fan-out** (Phases A/B, partitioned by concern) and the **adversarial verifiers** (Stage 3, Phase G) |
| Scorer (pass, or return to implementer) | **Does not exist as a role.** Stage 1 is the nearest analogue and it sits *before* the builder, not after |
| Tracker (feeds improvements back mid-flight) | **Does not exist.** "Wave1 audit the audit" (agent 24) is a retrospective, run after the loop had already collapsed |

---

# 2. THE ROLE PROMPTS

## 2.1 The scope-partitioned auditor (Phase A/B) — the highest-value reusable block

```
You are Agent B of a code-quality audit on repo <path>, branch <branch>.

YOUR SCOPE: **Import analysis only.** Do not audit naming, TypeScript typing,
or test coverage.

Read .claude/rules/conventions.md ("Imports" section) and
.claude/rules/overrideStyling.md (the section "Importing an already-overridden
component from a new component") first.

[numbered checks, ending with:]
6. **THE BIG ONE — base-path vs relative import of an already-overridden component.**
   ...

CRITICAL — accuracy requirements:
1. Give `file:line` for every finding.
2. **Distinguish pre-existing from new** — run `git diff origin/develop -- <file>`
   before flagging. If the offending line is NOT an added line in this branch's
   diff, label it PRE-EXISTING. This matters a lot — do not report inherited debt
   as a new violation.
3. For check 6, actually verify the override directory exists with `ls` before
   reporting. A base-path import of a component with NO local override is CORRECT
   and must not be flagged.
4. Do not invent findings. "No issues" is valid.

Report only verified findings, each classified MUST-FIX / SHOULD-FIX / BACKLOG.
Do not modify files.
```

The **accuracy-requirements block appears in 15 prompts and evolves visibly**. By Phase B it has become a confession log:

```
ACCURACY REQUIREMENTS — this session has already produced several findings that
were artefacts of the checking method, so:
- Run `git diff origin/develop -- <file>` before flagging. `overrides/app/
  components/header/index.tsx` is the trap: its entire diff is 14 comment lines,
  but the file contains older violations.
- An annotated provisional constant (a raw value with a comment naming the open
  question / pending designer sign-off) is EXPLICITLY COMPLIANT per
  overrideStyling.md. Check for the comment before flagging.
- For `parts` vs `baseStyle` consistency, VERIFY AT RUNTIME (`npx tsx -e "..."`).
  A static regex on this file gives a wrong answer — I have made that mistake twice.
- Do not report a proxy as a finding. If a check returns a count, establish what
  the count actually means before drawing a conclusion.
```

And, verbatim from the test-coverage auditor:

```
- COVERAGE THROUGH A CONSUMER COUNTS. testing.md says pick the cheapest layer that
  proves the behaviour; a slot prop is correctly covered by the molecule that fills
  it, not the atom exposing it. Before flagging something untested, check whether a
  consumer's story or test exercises it, and report where the coverage actually lives.
  I previously reported `trailing` as uncovered when three `play` functions in
  ZimmInputAction exercise it.
- A case-sensitive grep miss is not absence — retry case-insensitively. I previously
  concluded "no story references the clear button" from a case-sensitive grep for
  "Clear input" while the story matched /clear input/i, and broke CI.
```

Also from the test auditor, the single best test-quality question in the session:

```
Part 2 — DO THE TESTS ACTUALLY HAVE VALUE? This is the more important half.
For each significant assertion, ask: **"would this test still pass if the feature
were broken in the obvious way?"** Flag any assertion that:
- asserts the ABSENCE of a feature (encoding a placeholder as expected behaviour,
  so it FAILS when the feature is correctly implemented later)
- is vacuous (iterates an empty collection, asserts a tautology, or `toBeTruthy()`
  as the sole assertion)
- tests the framework rather than our code
- duplicates coverage that a cheaper layer already provides
```

## 2.2 STAGE 1 — the prover

```
STAGE 1 of a 4-stage pipeline on <repo>, branch <branch>.

YOUR JOB: independently VALIDATE OR DISPROVE four claims by EXECUTION, not by
reading. You are the proof stage — a later agent will implement fixes only for
claims you confirm. Do NOT fix anything. Do NOT commit. READ-ONLY except for
temporary probe files you delete afterwards (verify `git status` is clean before
you finish).

Allowed: `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npx vitest run`, `npx tsx -e`, `npx eslint`, `node`,
git read commands, temporary probe files under overrides/ that you delete.
FORBIDDEN: `npm start`, `npm run build-storybook`, `npx test-storybook` (another
process owns those and a concurrent build collides). Do not modify any tracked file.

=== CLAIM M1 ===
<claim stated in full>
PROVE by: copying the file, deleting both casts, compiling under the project
tsconfig. Then separately prove or disprove the widening/XOR claim — construct a
probe that would be REJECTED with the XOR intact and check whether it is accepted
with the casts present.

FOR EACH CLAIM output: **CONFIRMED** / **DISPROVED** / **PARTIALLY CONFIRMED**, the
exact command(s) and their output as evidence, and — if confirmed — the minimal
correct fix with the reason it is minimal. If a claim is overstated in any part, say
precisely which part. A disproved claim is a valuable result; do not manufacture
confirmation.

End with `git status --porcelain` output proving you left the tree clean.
```

The later Stage 1 prompts add a **viability gate**, which is the thing that saved the pipeline:

```
FOR EACH: CONFIRMED / DISPROVED / PARTIALLY CONFIRMED, commands and output as
evidence, and — if confirmed — the minimal fix PLUS an explicit viability verdict
(is the proposed fix actually implementable without changing a public API or
breaking rendering?). Distinguish what you proved by execution from what you inferred.
```

And a pre-emptive self-correction, from the TypeScript audit prompt:

```
- If you propose a type predicate anywhere, check it is SOUND first.
  `isSafeHref(href): href is string` is UNSOUND — 'javascript:void(0)' is a string
  that returns false, so the false branch would narrow to `undefined` incorrectly.
  That was evaluated and deliberately rejected in favour of widening the caller.
```

## 2.3 STAGE 2 — the implementer

```
STAGE 2 (implementation) of a 4-stage pipeline. Repo <path>, branch <branch>.
Stage 1 already PROVED every claim below by execution — your job is to implement
and prove the fix works, not to re-litigate whether the problem is real.

FILE OWNERSHIP — you may modify ONLY these two files. Two sibling agents are working
concurrently on other files; touching anything else will collide.
  overrides/app/theme/components/recipeGuards.test.ts
  overrides/app/theme/components/zimmTextInput.ts

DO NOT COMMIT. DO NOT `git add`. Leave changes in the working tree.
FORBIDDEN: `npm start`, `npm run build-storybook`, `npx test-storybook` (a later
stage owns those). Allowed: `npx vitest run`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npx tsx -e`,
`npx eslint`, `npx prettier`, node, git reads.

=== S1 — recipeGuards' three guards pass vacuously on empty input (PROVEN) ===
<evidence restated>
IMPLEMENT: <exact code>
PROVE: show it passes normally, and show it FAILS when you temporarily stub
`components` to `{}` (then restore).
```

Three devices in these prompts carry most of the weight:

**(a) Explicit negative scope with the reason:**
```
**DO NOT touch the `input` part (~line 112).** Stage 1 proved that would be a
REGRESSION: the input currently INHERITS `lineHeight: 21px`, and
`textStyle:'body2'` would SET it to 18px, moving the glyph baseline inside a fixed
20px box. Leave it alone.
```

**(b) A ✅/❌ scope table:**
```
SCOPE — do exactly this and no more:
  ✅ Move `display`, `width`, `maxWidth`, `height`, `overflow` into a new
     `theme/components/zimmLogo.ts` recipe, consumed via `useStyleConfig`...
  ✅ Keep the `...style` prop-forwarding override working — it must still win.
  ✅ Fix the FALSE comment at :21-23.
  ❌ DO NOT change the `useToken` call or the colour handling. ... OUT OF SCOPE.
  ❌ DO NOT resolve `LOGO_MAX_WIDTH`/`LOGO_HEIGHT` to different values.
```

**(c) A measured baseline the fix must preserve:**
```
BASELINE YOU MUST PRESERVE (Stage 1 measured, live dev server, footer):
  desktop 1440: display:block · width:327px · maxWidth:327px · height:39px ·
                overflow:clip · rect 327 × 39
  mobile   390: rect 326 × 39   ← so `width:100%` IS load-bearing below the 327px
                cap; do not drop it
PROVE by measuring against the dev server before and after and showing every one of
those values is unchanged at BOTH widths. If any value moves, your fix is wrong —
say so rather than accepting it.
```

**(d) Mandatory mutation testing — the single best line in the whole corpus:**
```
CRITICAL: mutation-test your new assertions. Temporarily break the trap (e.g. make
the keydown handler return early) and the scroll lock (remove the overflow write)

## The 4-stage pipeline ran exactly ONE round. It never looped.

**The loop lived one stage earlier than designed.** Stage 1 is where rejection happened — *before* implementation, not after:

- **M1 — PARTIALLY CONFIRMED.** Parts A and B confirmed; part C **DISPROVED**: *"'erase the XOR guarantee of `ZimmIconProps`': DISPROVED. With the casts present, every invalid call site is still rejected... The widening is real but **inert**."*
- **S3 — CONFIRMED, but the fix rejected.** *"**Where the claim is wrong:** 'carry the last non-index key forward' only fixes the **array** form. Responsive-object keys (`base`, `md`) are not numeric indices, so `width: {base:'xl'}` still escapes — 3 of 18 cases still wrong. Verified by execution."* Stage 1 then **built and validated a replacement**, scored `0 incorrect of 18` against 10 deliberate false-positive controls.

# 4. WHAT THE TESTER CHECKED

Testing was never one role. It was **three separable layers**, and they had very different hit rates.

### Layer 1 — Static audit, partitioned by concern (10 agents)

The angles, verbatim from the prompts:

| Angle | The specific trap it was told to hunt |
|---|---|
| **Imports** | "base-path import of an already-overridden component... the real app build resolves to the override but Storybook and Vitest resolve to BASE. The story/test then silently exercises the wrong component." |
| **Imports** | "The four path-alias configs must agree — babel.config.js, tsconfig.json, .storybook/main.js, vitest.config.ts... a mismatch silently breaks one environment only." |
| **Imports** | "Bridge pattern — grep whether SFCC's own base components import it... Any hits ⇒ the default export must stay a faithful undecorated port." |
| **Tokens/CSS** | "**The sizing-vs-spacing trap.** The Zimmermann named scale is registered as `theme.space` ONLY. A bare scale key on width/height/boxSize falls through to Chakra's `sizes` — a silent 20-30x blow-up." |
| **Tokens/CSS** | "Shorthand-after-longhand inside a theme recipe (e.g. `paddingBlock` then `padding: 0` wipes it)." |
| **Tokens/CSS** | "extendTheme deep-merge. Recipe keys must be namespaced when fully rewriting a base SFCC recipe." |
| **TypeScript** | "`any` without justification; `satisfies` over `as`; `readonly` where the receiver must not mutate; discriminated unions for variant/state modelling" |
| **Tests** | "would this test still pass if the feature were broken in the obvious way?" |
| **AC conformance** | AC-by-AC verdict SATISFIED / PARTIALLY / NOT / **OUT OF SCOPE BY THE STORY'S OWN TEXT**, plus "**Anything BUILT THAT THE STORY DOES NOT ASK FOR.** Scope creep is as much a finding as a gap." |

### Layer 2 — Execution proof (Stage 1, Stage 3, the fresh-eyes verifiers)

Measurement against a **running dev server via Playwright**, at 1440/768/390/375/320; probe files compiled under the project tsconfig then deleted; theme objects imported and rendered through a real `ChakraProvider`; **mutation controls on every instrument**.

### Layer 3 — Browser-truth (Stage 3 only)

`build-storybook` + `test-storybook --ci` + axe. Deliberately forbidden to every other agent to avoid port collisions.

# 6. THE PASS CRITERIA

**"Done" was defined four different ways, and only one of them was mechanical.**

### The mechanical gate — the only consistent one

Established by an audit agent that found the two governing docs disagreed:

> *"| Playbook, Play 5 'Gate zero' | `npx tsc --noEmit` · `npm run lint` · `npx vitest run` — **3** |*
> *| Manual §8 | ...**plus** `npm run build-storybook && npx test-storybook` · `/code-quality` · `coderabbit ... --light --base develop` ('**required, not optional**') — **6** |*
> *The manual is the fuller set and is the one I audited against. The gap is material: **'Vitest does not run `play` functions.** A change that breaks a story passes `npm test` and fails in CI. That happened on the footer PR.' A developer following the playbook's gate zero on this very branch would have shipped that failure."*

Stage 3 turned that into a **numeric pass/fail table with baselines stated in the prompt**:

```
| `npx tsc --noEmit`         | 0 errors, exit 0        | PASS
| `npx vitest run`           | **190/190**, 9 files    | PASS — exact match
| `npm run lint`             | 19 errors + 3 warnings  | PASS — byte-identical to baseline
| `npx prettier --check` ×12 | all clean               | PASS
| `npm run build-storybook`  | exit 0                  | PASS
| `npx test-storybook --ci`  | **76/76, 12 suites**    | PASS — exact match
| axe-core (bonus)           | 0 violations, 23 passes | PASS
```

Two things make this the strongest gate in the session:
1. **Every number was pre-declared in the prompt** — the agent couldn't rationalise a delta.
2. **Pre-existing failures were baselined by blob hash**, not by count: *"`definitions.ts` and `routes.tsx` verified byte-identical to `origin/develop` by blob hash. **ANY error outside those files is new and is a regression.**"*

### The proof gate (Stage 1)
`CONFIRMED / DISPROVED / PARTIALLY CONFIRMED`, plus a **clean-tree receipt**: *"End with `git status --porcelain` output proving you left the tree clean."* And explicitly: *"A disproved claim is a valuable result; do not manufacture confirmation."*

### The severity gate (audits)
`MUST-FIX / SHOULD-FIX / BACKLOG`, plus a mandatory **"verified clean / deliberately not flagged" section so items don't get re-raised.** Phase G swapped in `CLAIM TRUE / FALSE / PARTLY` → `FIX / DECLINE / DEFER`, with the rule: *"If DECLINE: the specific quotable repo rule, doc, or empirical result — **not an opinion**."*

### The consistency gate — inconsistent by design
`UPHELD / OVERTURNED / RAISE WITH TIM` (precedent audits) and `WRONG / STALE / OVERSTATED / UNVERIFIABLE / SPOT-CHECKED OK` (fact-checks).

**Was it consistent? No — five different vocabularies across seven phases.** But the disagreement is mostly principled: proof (binary), severity (triage), precedent (authority), fact (accuracy). The genuine gap is that **nothing ever combined them into one "this step is done" judgement.** That is precisely the scorer role Marcel remembers and that never existed.

**The most important judgement in the session was made by an agent, not a gate:**
> *"| Window | Commits/items | B/C-dominant | Yield |*
> *| 08-17 → 08-20 | 38 commits | 21 | **55%** |*
> *| 08-21, committed (to 16:51) | 17 commits | 8 | **47%** |*
> *| **Final pass (uncommitted)** | **13 items** | **1** | **8%** |*
> *Marginal value fell ~6× at one identifiable point: **after `9ec0740`, 2026-08-21 16:51.** ... The collapse is not gradual. **It is one pass.**"*

And its diagnosis of the session's root failure mode:
> *"**the verification instrument was built from the same belief as the thing it verified, and was never made to fail on purpose.**"*

Wave 2 corroborated with the sharpest line in the corpus:

**C. The non-vacuity clause** — generalise S1 into a standing rule:
```
Before asserting a collection is empty, assert the collector found something.
`expect(offenders).toEqual([])` is satisfied by an empty input. Add a `> 0` floor —
never pin an exact count, it churns on every legitimate edit.
```

**D. The measured baseline block:**
```
BASELINE YOU MUST PRESERVE (measured, live dev server):
  <viewport>: <every value>
PROVE by measuring before and after and showing every one of those values is
unchanged. If any value moves, your fix is wrong — say so rather than accepting it.
```

**E. The ✅/❌ scope table** with a reason on every ❌, and:
```
If you judge <item> NOT worth doing after attempting it, say so with evidence —
a reasoned decline is an acceptable outcome.
```

**F. The accuracy-requirements block** (adapt the specifics per project, keep the shape):
```
ACCURACY REQUIREMENTS — I have made these mistakes:
- Distinguish PRE-EXISTING from NEW: run `git diff <base> -- <file>` before flagging.
- Verify by execution, not by reading, wherever you can. A static regex on <X> gives
  a wrong answer.
- A case-sensitive grep miss is not absence — retry case-insensitively.
- Coverage through a CONSUMER counts. Before flagging something untested, check
  whether a consumer exercises it, and report where the coverage actually lives.
- **Do not report a proxy as a finding.** If a check returns a count, establish what
  the count actually means before drawing a conclusion.
- Do not invent findings. "No issues" is valid.
```

**G. The Stage-3 adversary framing**, with pre-declared numeric baselines and this line:
```
Three sibling agents just implemented N fixes in parallel, partitioned by file. They
have ALL FINISHED — you have exclusive access. You are the adversary, not the advocate.

=== THE INTERACTION RISKS I WANT YOU TO HUNT ===
Agents A and C BOTH touched <shared surface>. Specifically:
1. <risk>. They reported <claim> — verify independently against the CURRENT tree,
   not their snapshot.
```

**H. The fresh-eyes clause** — used ~12 times, and it worked every time:
```
You have NO prior context — that is deliberate. Verify everything from scratch. Do
not assume any claim is true because it is confidently written / because the change
looks deliberate.
```

**I. The suspicion heuristic:**
```
This was added so a failing check would pass. That is inherently suspicious — a test
was failing and a change was made that causes it to stop failing. Does the change
make the check assert something WEAKER than before?
```

**J. The convention-vs-fact distinction** (from the precedent auditor) — the cleanest rule in the corpus for handling disagreement with an authority.

**K. The port/artefact-collision protocol** — verbatim, including the md5 comparison and the negative control.

**L. The test-value question:**
```
"Would this test still pass if the feature were broken in the obvious way?"
Flag any assertion that: asserts the ABSENCE of a feature; is vacuous; tests the
framework rather than our code; duplicates coverage a cheaper layer already provides.
```

**M. The scope ledger's five-category forcing function** — `[R] REQUIRED / [S] SUPPORTING / [D] DEFERRED / [U] UNMENTIONED`, with:
```
[S] is the category most open to abuse — for every [S], state what would BREAK
without it. If nothing breaks, it is [U].
Quote the story text when you assign [D]. Do not assign [D] from memory.
Do not editorialise about quality. A well-built [U] is still [U].
```

**N. The self-critique prompt**, run *during* the loop rather than after it — this is the tracker role Marcel remembers, and it should be scheduled, not retrospective:
```
Be genuinely critical. I am the one who ran this loop and I am asking whether it was
worth it. A defensive answer is useless to me; so is a performatively harsh one.
I want the real curve.
Classify every fix: [B] behaviour / [C] correctness / [T] test-guard / [Y] type-only
/ [X] cosmetic. Give the ratio.
"Be more careful" is not an answer.
```

## 7.2 Do NOT carry forward

**1. Stage 4.** Named in the design, never spawned. Either build a real scorer/commit agent or drop it from the description — a phantom stage teaches the wrong shape.

**2. The scorer-loops-back-to-implementer topology.** It never happened. The productive loop is **prove-before-implement** (Stage 1 → Stage 2), which rejected ~1 in 3 claim-parts. Encode that. A post-hoc scorer with a return path is an untested idea.

**3. Running the same partitioned audit twice.** Phases A and B are ~3 hours of duplicate work for marginal delta.

**4. Guards written for failure modes that haven't occurred on the surface the guard can see.** 0-for-3 versus 3-for-3. The rule to encode: *write the guard after the defect ships, on the surface where it shipped.*

**5. Any check that cannot see JSX/`sx` props, sold as coverage.** The theme walker was extended twice while the only live instance of the class it guards sat in a file it structurally cannot reach. The guard file said so and the loop built it anyway.

**6. Fanning out on a decided question.** Four agents on `vi.clearAllMocks()`; three on kebab-case with a written withdrawal already on record. Add a **precedent-check step before dispatch**: has this been settled, and where.

**7. Multi-agent write access to one working tree without a coordinator.** Six documented collisions. If parallel writes are needed, mandate git worktrees; if reads must be trustworthy, mandate `git show HEAD:<path>`.

**8. Auditing your own conclusions.** The measured inflection: *"positive marginal value while it was reading code and negative value once it began reading its own conclusions."* Encode a stop rule — e.g. *stop when a pass yields <20% behaviour/correctness items*, which is exactly where this session's collapse showed up (8%).

**9. A loop scoped to the working tree only.** Everything that mattered and got missed lived outside it: review threads, licence terms, project-state docs, and the one AC the story explicitly called out. Any reusable skill needs an explicit outside-the-tree sweep as a first-class step, not an afterthought.
